sub_structure.5: (5) No company shall issue a prospectus or make an offer or invitation to the public or to its members exceeding five hundred for the subscription of its debentures, unless the company has, before such issue or offer, appointed one or more debenture trustees...[cite: 17]
sub_structure.10: (10) Where a company fails to redeem the debentures on the date of their maturity or fails to pay interest... the Tribunal may, on the application of any or all of the debenture-holders... direct, by order, the company to redeem the debentures forthwith...[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: Authorizes debt instruments and convertible debentures (common in venture debt). Debentures can never carry voting rights. Offers extended to more than 500 subscribers require appointing a registered Debenture Trustee.[cite: 17]

title: Power to nominate
text: (1) Every holder of securities of a company may, at any time, nominate, in the prescribed manner, any person to whom his securities shall vest in the event of his death.[cite: 17]

sub_structure.3: (3) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force or in any disposition, whether testamentary or otherwise... where a nomination made in the prescribed manner purports to confer on any person the right to vest the securities... the nominee shall, on the death of the holder... become entitled to all the rights in the securities... to the exclusion of all other persons...[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: Allows security holders to legally register a nominee who will inherit and control their shares or debentures upon death, taking precedence over general succession disputes until legally determined.[cite: 17]

title: Prohibition on acceptance of deposits from public
text: (1) On and after the commencement of this Act, no company shall invite, accept or renew deposits under this Act from the public except in a manner provided under this Chapter: Provided that nothing in this sub-section shall apply to a banking company and non-banking financial company...[cite: 17]

sub_structure.2: (2) A company may, subject to the passing of a resolution in general meeting and subject to such rules as may be prescribed... accept deposits from its members on such terms and conditions... subject to the fulfilment of the following conditions, namely:- (a) issuance of a circular to its members... (c) depositing, on or before the thirtieth day of April each year, such sum which shall not be less than twenty per cent. of the amount of its deposits maturing during the following financial year...[cite: 17]
sub_structure.4: (4) Where a company fails to repay the deposit or part thereof or any interest thereon... the depositor concerned may apply to the Tribunal for an order directing the company to pay the sum due...[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: General companies and startups are strictly banned from taking public deposits. A company can accept limited deposits from its own members/shareholders, but only after circularizing credit ratings, maintaining a 20% deposit repayment reserve, and passing member resolutions.[cite: 17]

title: Repayment of deposits, etc., accepted before commencement of this Act
text: (1) Where in respect of any deposit accepted by a company before the commencement of this Act, the amount of such deposit or part thereof or any interest due thereon remains unpaid... the company shall- (a) file, within a period of three months... with the Registrar a statement of all the deposits accepted... and (b) repay within three years from such commencement or on or before expiry of the period for which the deposits were accepted, whichever is earlier...[cite: 17]

sub_structure.3: (3) If a company fails to repay the deposit or part thereof or any interest thereon within the time specified... the company shall, in addition to the payment of the amount... be punishable with fine which shall not be less than one crore rupees but which may extend to ten crore rupees and every officer... shall be punishable with imprisonment which may extend to seven years or with fine which shall not be less than twenty-five lakh rupees but which may extend to two crore rupees, or with both.[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: Transitional rules requiring companies that held public deposits when the 2013 Act arrived to register statements and clear all repayment dues. Failure to repay triggers fines up to ₹10 Crore and prison terms up to 7 years.[cite: 17]

title: Damages for fraud
text: (1) Where a company fails to repay the deposit or part thereof or any interest thereon referred to in section 74... and it is proved that the deposits had been accepted with intent to defraud the depositors or for any fraudulent purpose, every officer of the company who was responsible for the acceptance of such deposit shall, without prejudice to the provisions contained in sub-section (3) of that section and liability under section 447, be personally responsible, without any limitation of liability, for all or any of the losses or damages that may have been incurred by the depositors.[cite: 17]

sub_structure.2: (2) Any suit, proceedings or other action may be taken by any person, group of persons or any association of persons who had incurred any loss as a result of the failure of the company to repay the deposits...[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: If deposits were accepted fraudulently to swindle depositors, the corporate veil is pierced: responsible officers and directors face unlimited personal liability for every rupee lost, on top of criminal prosecution under Section 447.[cite: 17]

title: Acceptance of deposits from public by certain companies
text: (1) Notwithstanding anything contained in section 73, a public company, having such net worth or turnover as may be prescribed, may accept deposits from persons other than its members subject to compliance with the requirements provided in sub-section (2) of section 73 and subject to such rules as the Central Government may, in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India, prescribe: Provided that such a company shall be required to obtain the rating... from a recognised credit rating agency...[cite: 17]

sub_structure.1_proviso_2: Provided further that every company accepting secured deposits from the public shall within thirty days of such acceptance, create a charge on its assets of an amount not less than the amount of deposits accepted...[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: Only large public companies meeting prescribed net worth or turnover thresholds can accept public deposits. They must maintain annual credit ratings from certified rating agencies and secure the deposits with a charge over assets within 30 days.[cite: 17]

title: Punishment for contravention of section 73 or section 76
text: Where a company accepts or invites or allows or causes any other person to accept or invite on its behalf any deposit in contravention of the manner or the conditions prescribed under section 73 or section 76 or rules made thereunder or if a company fails to repay the deposit or part thereof or any interest due thereon... (a) the company shall... be punishable with fine which shall not be less than one crore rupees or twice the amount of deposit accepted by the company, whichever is lower but which may extend to ten crore rupees; and (b) every officer of the company who is in default shall be punishable with imprisonment which may extend to seven years and with fine which shall not be less than twenty-five lakh rupees but which may extend to two crore rupees...[cite: 17]

sub_structure.proviso: Provided that if it is proved that the officer of the company who is in default, has contravened such provisions knowingly or wilfully with the intention to deceive the company or its shareholders or depositors or creditors or tax authorities, he shall be liable for action under section 447.[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: Prescribes harsh penalties for illegal deposit schemes. The company faces fines up to ₹10 Crore, while defaulting officers face up to 7 years in prison and fines up to ₹2 Crore, escalated to Section 447 fraud penalties if deliberate deception is proven.[cite: 17]

title: Duty to register charges, etc.
text: (1) It shall be the duty of every company creating a charge within or outside India, on its property or assets or any of its undertakings, whether tangible or otherwise, and situated in or outside India, to register the particulars of the charge signed by the company and the charge-holder together with the instruments... with the Registrar within thirty days of its creation:[cite: 17]

sub_structure.1_proviso_b: (b) in case of charges created on or after the commencement of the Companies (Amendment) Act, 2019, within a period of sixty days of such creation, on payment of such additional fees as may be prescribed:[cite: 17]
sub_structure.3: (3) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, no charge created by a company shall be taken into account by the liquidator appointed under this Act or the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016... or any other creditor unless it is duly registered under sub-section (1) and a certificate of registration... is given by the Registrar...[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: Whenever a startup pledges assets or takes bank loans/venture debt securing company collateral, it must register this 'charge' with the ROC within 30 days (extendable to 60). Unregistered charges are completely invalid against liquidators and bankruptcy trustees under the IBC.[cite: 17]

title: Application for registration of charge
text: Where a company fails to register the charge within the period of thirty days referred to in sub-section (1) of section 77 without prejudice to its liability in respect of any offence under this Chapter, the person in whose favour the charge is created may apply to the Registrar for registration of the charge along with the instrument created for the charge, within such time and in such form and manner as may be prescribed...[cite: 17]

sub_structure.proviso: Provided that where registration is effected on application of the person in whose favour the charge is created, that person shall be entitled to recover from the company the amount of any fees or additional fees paid by him to the Registrar for the purpose of registration of charge.[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: If a startup neglects to file and register a loan charge within 30 days, the lender or charge-holder has the legal right to apply directly to the Registrar to record the charge and recover all registration and penalty fees from the company.[cite: 17]

title: Section 77 to apply in certain matters
text: The provisions of section 77 relating to registration of charges shall, so far as may be, apply to- (a) a company acquiring any property subject to a charge within the meaning of that section; or (b) any modification in the terms or conditions or the extent or operation of any charge registered under that section.[cite: 17]
plain_english_summary: If a startup buys property that already has a loan attached to it, or if they modify the terms of an existing bank loan, they must file and register these changes with the ROC just like a brand new charge.[cite: 17]

title: Date of notice of charge
text: Where any charge on any property or assets of a company or any of its undertakings is registered under section 77, any person acquiring such property, assets, undertakings or part thereof or any share or interest therein shall be deemed to have notice of the charge from the date of such registration.[cite: 17]
plain_english_summary: Once a startup registers a loan charge on its assets with the ROC, it is legally assumed that the entire public knows about it. No buyer can claim they 'didn't know' the asset was pledged to a bank.[cite: 17]

title: Register of charges to be kept by Registrar
text: (1) The Registrar shall, in respect of every company, keep a register containing particulars of the charges registered under this Chapter in such form and in such manner as may be prescribed.[cite: 17]

sub_structure.2: (2) A register kept in pursuance of this section shall be open to inspection by any person on payment of such fees as may be prescribed for each inspection.[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: The Registrar of Companies (ROC) maintains a master public registry of all loans and charges against every company. Anyone, including future investors, can pay a small fee to inspect this list.[cite: 17]

title: Company to report satisfaction of charge
text: (1) A company shall give intimation to the Registrar in the prescribed form, of the payment or satisfaction in full of any charge registered under this Chapter within a period of thirty days from the date of such payment or satisfaction...[cite: 17]

sub_structure.1_proviso: Provided that the Registrar may, on an application by the company or the charge holder, allow such intimation of payment or satisfaction to be made within a period of three hundred days... on payment of such additional fees...[cite: 17]
sub_structure.2: (2) The Registrar shall, on receipt of intimation under sub-section (1), cause a notice to be sent to the holder of the charge calling upon him to show cause within such time not exceeding fourteen days... as to why payment or satisfaction in full should not be recorded...[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: When a startup fully pays off a bank loan or debt, it must notify the ROC within 30 days so the charge can be officially cleared from its records. The ROC will double-check with the lender before clearing it.[cite: 17]

title: Power of Registrar to make entries of satisfaction and release in absence of intimation from company
text: (1) The Registrar may, on evidence being given to his satisfaction with respect to any registered charge,- (a) that the debt for which the charge was given has been paid or satisfied in whole or in part; or (b) that part of the property or undertaking charged has been released... enter in the register of charges a memorandum of satisfaction... notwithstanding the fact that no intimation has been received by him from the company.[cite: 17]
plain_english_summary: If a startup forgets to report that a loan was paid off, the ROC can still clear the charge from the public register if they receive strong independent evidence that the debt was settled or the property released.[cite: 17]

title: Intimation of appointment of receiver or manager
text: (1) If any person obtains an order for the appointment of a receiver of, or of a person to manage, the property, subject to a charge, of a company or if any person appoints such receiver or person under any power contained in any instrument, he shall, within a period of thirty days... give notice of such appointment to the company and the Registrar...[cite: 17]
plain_english_summary: If a lender forces the appointment of a receiver or manager to take over a defaulting startup's pledged assets, the lender must notify the ROC within 30 days so the public record reflects this hostile takeover of the asset.[cite: 17]

title: Company's register of charges
text: (1) Every company shall keep at its registered office a register of charges in such form and in such manner as may be prescribed, which shall include there in all charges and floating charges affecting any property or assets of the company...[cite: 17]

sub_structure.2: (2) The register of charges and instrument of charges... shall be open for inspection during business hours- (a) by any member or creditor without any payment of fees; or (b) by any other person on payment of such fees as may be prescribed...[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: In addition to the government's registry, the startup itself must maintain its own internal 'Register of Charges' at its head office, alongside copies of the loan documents. Shareholders and creditors can inspect this for free.[cite: 17]

title: Punishment for contravention
text: (1) If any company is in default in complying with any of the provisions of this Chapter, the company shall be liable to a penalty of five lakh rupees and every officer of the company who is in default shall be liable to a penalty of fifty thousand rupees.[cite: 17]

sub_structure.2: (2) If any person willfully furnishes any false or incorrect information or knowingly suppresses any material information, required to be registered in accordance with the provisions of section 77, he shall be liable for action under section 447.[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: Strict penalties for messing up loan registrations: Startups face a ₹5 Lakh fine and defaulting officers face a ₹50,000 fine. Intentionally hiding or faking loan information is treated as criminal corporate fraud under Section 447.[cite: 17]

title: Rectification by Central Government in Register of charges
text: The Central Government on being satisfied that- (a) the omission to give intimate to the Registrar of the payment or satisfaction of a charge, within the time required... or (b) the omission or misstatement of any particulars... was accidental or due to inadvertence or some other sufficient cause or it is not of a nature to prejudice the position of creditors or shareholders... it may, on the application of the company... direct that the time for the giving of intimation of payment... shall be extended or... that the omission or misstatement shall be rectified.[cite: 17]
plain_english_summary: If a startup makes an honest mistake or misses a deadline regarding loan registrations, they can apply to the Central Government to pardon the delay or fix the typo, as long as it wasn't done to cheat investors or lenders.[cite: 17]

title: Register of members, etc.
text: (1) Every company shall keep and maintain the following registers in such form and in such manner as may be prescribed, namely:- (a) register of members indicating separately for each class of equity and preference shares held by each member residing in or outside India; (b) register of debenture-holders; and (c) register of any other security holders.[cite: 17]

sub_structure.3: (3) The register and index of beneficial owners maintained by a depository under section 11 of the Depositories Act, 1996... shall be deemed to be the corresponding register and index for the purposes of this Act.[cite: 17]
sub_structure.5: (5) If a company does not maintain a register of members or debenture-holders... the company shall be liable to a penalty of three lakh rupees and every officer of the company who is in default shall be liable to a penalty of fifty thousand rupees.[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: This is the legal foundation for a startup's 'Cap Table'. A startup must officially maintain a Register of Members detailing exactly who owns what shares. Failing to maintain this accurately carries a strict ₹3 Lakh fine for the company.[cite: 17]

title: Declaration in respect of beneficial interest in any share
text: (1) Where the name of a person is entered in the register of members of a company as the holder of shares in that company but who does not hold the beneficial interest in such shares, such person shall make a declaration within such time and in such form as may be prescribed... specifying the name and other particulars of the person who holds the beneficial interest...[cite: 17]

sub_structure.2: (2) Every person who holds or acquires a beneficial interest in share of a company shall make a declaration to the company specifying the nature of his interest...[cite: 17]
sub_structure.5: (5) If any person fails to make a declaration as required under sub-section (1) or sub-section (2) or sub-section (3), he shall be liable to a penalty of fifty thousand rupees and in case of continuing failure, with a further penalty of two hundred rupees for each day...[cite: 17]
sub_structure.6: (6) Where any declaration under this section is made to a company, the company shall make a note of such declaration in the register concerned and shall file... a return in the prescribed form with the Registrar...[cite: 17]
sub_structure.10: (10) For the purposes of this section and section 90, beneficial interest in a share includes, directly or indirectly... the right or entitlement of a person alone or together with any other person to (i) exercise or cause to be exercised any or all of the rights attached to such share; or (ii) receive or participate in any dividend...[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: If someone's name is on the cap table, but the shares actually belong to a silent partner or trust (the 'beneficial owner'), both the registered owner and the actual owner must declare this to the company, and the company must alert the government. Hiding true ownership triggers daily fines.[cite: 17]

title: Register of significant beneficial owners in a company
text: (1) Every individual, who acting alone or together, or through one or more persons or trust... holds beneficial interests, of not less than twenty-five per cent. or such other percentage as may be prescribed, in shares of a company or the right to exercise, or the actual exercising of significant influence or control... (herein referred to as "significant beneficial owner"), shall make a declaration to the company...[cite: 17]

sub_structure.2: (2) Every company shall maintain a register of the interest declared by individuals under sub-section (1)...[cite: 17]
sub_structure.4A: (4A) Every company shall take necessary steps to identify an individual who is a significant beneficial owner in relation to the company and require him to comply with the provisions of this section.[cite: 17]
sub_structure.7: (7) The company shall,- (a) where that person fails to give the company the information... apply to the Tribunal... for an order directing that the shares in question be subject to restrictions with regard to transfer of interest, suspension of all rights...[cite: 17]
sub_structure.10: (10) If any person fails to make a declaration as required under sub-section (1), he shall be liable to a penalty of fifty thousand rupees and in case of continuing failure, with a further penalty...[cite: 17]
sub_structure.11: (11) If a company, required to maintain register... fails to do so... the company shall be liable to a penalty of one lakh rupees...[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: The SBO Rule: Any individual who ultimately owns or controls 25% or more of a startup (even indirectly through offshore holding companies or trusts) must declare themselves. If they hide, the startup must investigate, and the Tribunal can freeze those shares entirely.[cite: 17]

title: Power to close register of members or debenture-holders or other security holders
text: (1) A company may close the register of members or the register of debenture-holders or the register of other security holders for any period or periods not exceeding in the aggregate forty-five days in each year, but not exceeding thirty days at any one time, subject to giving of previous notice of at least seven days... in such manner as may be prescribed.[cite: 17]

sub_structure.2: (2) If the register of members... is closed without giving the notice as provided in sub-section (1), or after giving shorter notice... or for a continuous or an aggregate period in excess of the limits... the company and every officer of the company who is in default shall be liable to a penalty of five thousand rupees for every day subject to a maximum of one lakh rupees during which the register is kept closed.[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: A startup can temporarily freeze its cap table (usually to calculate who gets dividends or voting rights), but they cannot freeze it for more than 30 consecutive days, or 45 days total per year. Breaking this rule results in daily fines up to ₹1 Lakh.[cite: 17]

title: Annual return
text: (1) Every company shall prepare a return (hereinafter referred to as the annual return) in the prescribed form containing the particulars as they stood on the close of the financial year regarding- (a) its registered office, principal business activities, particulars of its holding, subsidiary and associate companies; (b) its shares, debentures and other securities and shareholding pattern; ... (g) remuneration of directors and key managerial personnel;[cite: 17]

sub_structure.4: (4) Every company shall file with the Registrar a copy of the annual return, within sixty days from the date on which the annual general meeting is held...[cite: 17]
sub_structure.5: (5) If any company fails to file its annual return under sub-section (4), before the expiry of the period specified therein, such company and its every officer who is in default shall be liable to a penalty of ten thousand rupees and in case of continuing failure, with a further penalty of one hundred rupees for each day...[cite: 17]
sub_structure.6: (6) If a company secretary in practice certifies the annual return otherwise than in conformity with the requirements of this section or the rules made thereunder, he shall be liable to a penalty of two lakh rupees.[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: The Annual Return (MGT-7) is a mandatory health check document detailing the startup's cap table, directors, and salaries. It must be filed with the ROC within 60 days of the AGM. Failure to file triggers severe compounding daily penalties.[cite: 17]

title: Place of keeping and inspection of registers, returns, etc.
text: (1) The registers required to be kept and maintained by a company under section 88 and copies of the annual return filed under section 92 shall be kept at the registered office of the company: Provided that such registers or copies of return may also be kept at any other place in India in which more than one-tenth of the total number of members entered in the register of members reside, if approved by a special resolution passed at a general meeting of the company...[cite: 17]

sub_structure.2: (2) The registers and their indices... and the copies of all the returns shall be open for inspection by any member, debenture-holder... during business hours without payment of any fees...[cite: 17]
sub_structure.4: (4) If any inspection or the making of any extract or copy required under this section is refused, the company and every officer of the company who is in default shall be liable, for each such default, to a penalty of one thousand rupees for every day subject to a maximum of one lakh rupees during which the refusal or default continues.[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: A startup's official cap table and annual returns must normally be kept at its registered office, open for free inspection by any shareholder. Refusing a shareholder access to these records triggers daily fines up to ₹1 Lakh.[cite: 17]

title: Registers, etc., to be evidence
text: The registers, their indices and copies of annual returns maintained under sections 88 and 94 shall be prima facie evidence of any matter directed or authorised to be inserted therein by or under this Act.[cite: 17]
plain_english_summary: In any legal dispute (like a fight between co-founders over equity), the official Register of Members maintained by the company is treated by courts as the primary, presumptive proof of who owns what.[cite: 17]

title: Annual general meeting
text: (1) Every company other than a One Person Company shall in each year hold in addition to any other meetings, a general meeting as its annual general meeting and shall specify the meeting as such in the notices calling it, and not more than fifteen months shall elapse between the date of one annual general meeting of a company and that of the next:[cite: 17]

sub_structure.1_proviso_1: Provided that in case of the first annual general meeting, it shall be held within a period of nine months from the date of closing of the first financial year of the company and in any other case, within a period of six months, from the date of closing of the financial year:[cite: 17]
sub_structure.2: (2) Every annual general meeting shall be called during business hours, that is, between 9 a.m. and 6 p.m. on any day that is not a National Holiday and shall be held either at the registered office of the company or at some other place within the city, town or village in which the registered office of the company is situate:[cite: 17]
sub_structure.2_proviso_1: Provided that annual general meeting of an unlisted company may be held at any place in India if consent is given in writing or by electronic mode by all the members in advance:[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: Startups must hold an Annual General Meeting (AGM) every year during business hours (not on a National Holiday). The gap between two AGMs cannot exceed 15 months. Private startups can hold the AGM anywhere in India, provided 100% of shareholders agree in advance.[cite: 17]

title: Power of Tribunal to call annual general meeting
text: (1) If any default is made in holding the annual general meeting of a company under section 96, the Tribunal may, notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or the articles of the company, on the application of any member of the company, call, or direct the calling of, an annual general meeting of the company and give such ancillary or consequential directions as the Tribunal thinks expedient:[cite: 17]

sub_structure.1_proviso: Provided that such directions may include a direction that one member of the company present in person or by proxy shall be deemed to constitute a meeting.[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: If rogue founders refuse to hold an AGM, any shareholder can petition the Tribunal (NCLT). The NCLT can legally force the company to hold the meeting, even ruling that just one single shareholder showing up constitutes a legally valid AGM.[cite: 17]

title: Power of Tribunal to call meetings of members, etc.
text: (1) If for any reason it is impracticable to call a meeting of a company, other than an annual general meeting, in any manner in which meetings of the company may be called, or to hold or conduct the meeting of the company in the manner prescribed by this Act or the articles of the company, the Tribunal may, either suo motu or on the application of any director or member... order a meeting of the company to be called...[cite: 17]
plain_english_summary: If board deadlocks or founder disputes make it impossible to hold an Extraordinary General Meeting (EGM) normally, a director or shareholder can ask the Tribunal to step in and forcefully convene the meeting to resolve the deadlock.[cite: 17]

title: Punishment for default in complying with provisions of sections 96 to 98
text: If any default is made in holding a meeting of the company in accordance with section 96 or section 97 or section 98 or in complying with any directions of the Tribunal, the company and every officer of the company who is in default shall be punishable with fine which may extend to one lakh rupees and in the case of a continuing default, with a further fine which may extend to five thousand rupees for every day during which such default continues.[cite: 17]
plain_english_summary: Failing to hold the Annual General Meeting (AGM) on time, or ignoring a Tribunal order to hold a meeting, is a strict compliance violation. The startup faces fines up to ₹1 Lakh, plus ₹5,000 for every single day the delay continues.[cite: 17]

title: Calling of extraordinary general meeting
text: (1) The Board may, whenever it deems fit, call an extraordinary general meeting of the company.[cite: 17]

sub_structure.1_proviso: Provided that an extraordinary general meeting of the company, other than of the wholly owned subsidiary of a company incorporated outside India, shall be held at a place within India.[cite: 17]
sub_structure.2_a: (2) The Board shall, at the requisition made by,- (a) in the case of a company having a share capital, such number of members who hold, on the date of the receipt of the requisition, not less than one-tenth of such of the paid-up share capital of the company as on that date carries the right of voting... call an extraordinary general meeting of the company within the period specified in sub-section (4).[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: The Board of Directors can call an EGM at any time. Alternatively, shareholders holding at least 10% of the paid-up capital can force the Board to call an EGM to address urgent matters. EGMs must be held in India unless it's a wholly-owned subsidiary of a foreign company.[cite: 17]

title: Notice of meeting
text: (1) A general meeting of a company may be called by giving not less than clear twenty-one days' notice either in writing or through electronic mode in such manner as maybe prescribed:[cite: 17]

sub_structure.1_proviso_1: Provided that a general meeting may be called after giving shorter notice than that specified in this sub-section if consent, in writing or by electronic mode, is accorded thereto- (i) in the case of an annual general meeting, by not less than ninty-five per cent. of the members entitled to vote thereat...[cite: 17]
sub_structure.3: (3) The notice of every meeting of the company shall be given to- (a) every member of the company... (b) the auditor or auditors of the company; and (c) every director of the company.[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: Companies must give at least 21 days' clear notice before holding a general meeting, sending it to all shareholders, directors, and auditors. A meeting can be called with shorter notice only if 95% of the voting members agree to it in writing or electronically.[cite: 17]

title: Statement to be annexed to notice
text: (1) A statement setting out the following material facts concerning each item of special business to be transacted at a general meeting, shall be annexed to the notice calling such meeting, namely:-[cite: 17]

sub_structure.1_a: (a) the nature of concern or interest, financial or otherwise, if any, in respect of each items of (i) every director and the manager, if any; (ii) every other key managerial personnel; and (iii) relatives of the persons...[cite: 17]
sub_structure.5: (5) Without prejudice to the provisions of sub-section (4), if any default is made in complying with the provisions of this section, every promoter, director, manager or other key managerial personnel of the company who is in default shall be liable to a penalty of fifty thousand rupees or five times the amount of benefit accruing to the promoter, director... whichever is higher.[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: When calling a meeting for 'special business', the company must attach an explanatory statement disclosing all material facts and any financial interests of the directors or promoters in that business. Hiding this information carries a minimum fine of ₹50,000 or 5x the illicit profit made.[cite: 17]

title: Quorum for meetings
text: (1) Unless the articles of the company provide for a larger number,- (a) in case of a public company,- (i) five members personally present if the number of members as on the date of meeting is not more than one thousand... (b) in the case of a private company, two members personally present, shall be the quorum for a meeting of the company.[cite: 17]

sub_structure.2: (2) If the quorum is not present within half-an-hour from the time appointed for holding a meeting of the company- (a) the meeting shall stand adjourned to the same day in the next week at the same time and place, or to such other date and such other time and place as the Board may determine...[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: For a private startup's shareholder meeting to be legally valid, at least 2 members must be personally present (quorum). If the quorum isn't met within 30 minutes, the meeting is automatically adjourned to the following week.[cite: 17]

title: Chairman of meetings
text: (1) Unless the articles of the company otherwise provide, the members personally present at the meeting shall elect one of themselves to be the Chairman thereof on a show of hands.[cite: 17]

sub_structure.2: (2) If a poll is demanded on the election of the Chairman, it shall be taken forthwith in accordance with the provisions of this Act and the Chairman elected on a show of hands under sub-section (1) shall continue to be the Chairman of the meeting until some other person is elected as Chairman as a result of the poll...[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: Shareholders present at a meeting will elect one of themselves to act as the Chairman of that meeting via a show of hands, unless the startup's AOA specifies a different rule.[cite: 17]

title: Proxies
text: (1) Any member of a company entitled to attend and vote at a meeting of the company shall be entitled to appoint another person as a proxy to attend and vote at the meeting on his behalf:[cite: 17]

sub_structure.1_proviso_1: Provided that a proxy shall not have the right to speak at such meeting and shall not been titled to vote except on a poll:[cite: 17]
sub_structure.1_proviso_4: Provided also that a person appointed as proxy shall act on behalf of such member or number of members not exceeding fifty and such number of shares as may be prescribed.[cite: 17]
sub_structure.5: (5) If for the purpose of any meeting of a company, invitations to appoint as proxy a person... are issued at the company's expense to any member entitled to have a notice... every officer of the company who issues the invitation as aforesaid or authorises or permits their issue, shall be liable to a penalty of fifty thousand rupees...[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: Shareholders can appoint a 'proxy' to attend a meeting and vote for them. However, a proxy cannot speak at the meeting and can only vote if a formal 'poll' is taken. Companies cannot legally use company funds to solicit proxy votes for a specific person.[cite: 17]

title: Restriction on voting rights
text: (1) Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, the articles of a company may provide that no member shall exercise any voting right in respect of any shares registered in his name on which any calls or other sums presently payable by him have not been paid, or in regard to which the company has exercised any right of lien.[cite: 17]

sub_structure.2: (2) A company shall not, except on the grounds specified in sub-section (1), prohibit any member from exercising his voting right on any other ground.[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: A startup can block a shareholder from voting if they haven't paid the money they owe on their shares (unpaid calls) or if the company has a lien on those shares. No other reasons can be used to legally block a vote.[cite: 17]

title: Voting by show of hands
text: (1) At any general meeting, a resolution put to the vote of the meeting shall, unless a poll is demanded under section 109 or the voting is carried out electronically, be decided on a show of hands.[cite: 17]

sub_structure.2: (2) A declaration by the Chairman of the meeting of the passing of a resolution or otherwise by show of hands under sub-section (1) and an entry to that effect in the books containing the minutes... shall be conclusive evidence...[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: By default, voting at general meetings is done by a simple 'show of hands', unless members demand a formal poll or electronic voting is used.[cite: 17]

title: Voting through electronic means
text: The Central Government may prescribe the class or classes of companies and manner in which a member may exercise his right to vote by the electronic means.[cite: 17]
plain_english_summary: The government has the power to mandate that certain companies must provide their shareholders with an electronic (e-voting) platform to cast their votes.[cite: 17]

title: Demand for poll
text: (1) Before or on the declaration of the result of the voting on any resolution on show of hands, a poll may be ordered to be taken by the Chairman of the meeting on his own motion, and shall be ordered to be taken by him on a demand made in that behalf,- (a) in the case a company having a share capital, by the members present in person or by proxy, where allowed, and having not less than one-tenth of the total voting power or holding shares on which an aggregate sum of not less than five lakh rupees or such higher amount as may be prescribed has been paid-up;[cite: 17]

sub_structure.3: (3) A poll demanded for adjournment of the meeting or appointment of Chairman of the meeting shall be taken forthwith.[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: Shareholders holding at least 10% of the voting power (or ₹5 Lakhs paid-up capital) can demand a formal 'poll' (a rigorous vote counting shares rather than just a simple show of hands).[cite: 17]

title: Postal ballot
text: (1) Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, a company- (a) shall, in respect of such items of business as the Central Government may, by notification, declare to be transacted only by means of postal ballot; and (b) may, in respect of any item of business, other than ordinary business and any business in respect of which directors or auditors have a right to be heard at any meeting, transact by means of postal ballot, in such manner as may be prescribed, instead of transacting such business at a general meeting:[cite: 17]

sub_structure.2: (2) If a resolution is assented to by the requisite majority of the shareholders by means of postal ballot, it shall be deemed to have been duly passed at a general meeting convened in that behalf.[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: Companies can (and for certain items, must) ask shareholders to vote via mail or electronic postal ballot rather than requiring everyone to gather in a physical room for a meeting.[cite: 17]

title: Circulation of members' resolution
text: (1) A company shall, on requisition in writing of such number of members, as required in section 100,- (a) give notice to members of any resolution which may properly be moved and is intended to be moved at a meeting; and (b) circulate to members any statement with respect to the matters referred to in proposed resolution or business to be dealt with at that meeting.[cite: 17]

sub_structure.5: (5) If any default is made in complying with the provisions of this section, the company and every officer of the company who is in default shall be liable to a penalty of twenty-five thousand rupees.[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: If enough shareholders (who meet the 10% threshold) draft a resolution they want voted on, the company is legally required to circulate that resolution to all other shareholders. Ignoring this request costs the company a ₹25,000 fine.[cite: 17]

title: Representation of President and Governors in meetings
text: (1) The President of India or the Governor of a State, if he is a member of a company, may appoint such person as he thinks fit to act as his representative at any meeting of the company or at any meeting of any class of members of the company.[cite: 17]
plain_english_summary: If the Indian Government owns shares in a company, the President or Governor can appoint an official representative to attend meetings and vote on their behalf.[cite: 17]

title: Representation of corporations at meeting of companies and of creditors
text: (1) A body corporate, whether a company within the meaning of this Act or not, may, (a) if it is a member of a company within the meaning of this Act, by resolution of its Board of Directors or other governing body, authorise such person as it thinks fit to act as its representative at any meeting of the company, or at any meeting of any class of members of the company;[cite: 17]

sub_structure.2: (2) A person authorised by resolution under sub-section (1) shall be entitled to exercise the same rights and powers, including the right to vote by proxy and by postal ballot, on behalf of the body corporate which he represents...[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: If a VC fund or another company owns shares in your startup, they can pass a board resolution to appoint an official representative to attend your shareholder meetings and vote for them with full rights.[cite: 17]

title: Ordinary and special resolutions
text: (1) A resolution shall be an ordinary resolution if the notice required under this Act has been duly given and it is required to be passed by the votes cast, whether on a show of hands, or electronically or on a poll, as the case may be, in favour of the resolution, including the casting vote, if any, of the Chairman, by members who, being entitled so to do, vote in person, or where proxies are allowed, by proxy or by postal ballot, exceed the votes, if any, cast against the resolution by members, so entitled and voting.[cite: 17]

sub_structure.2_c: (2) A resolution shall be a special resolution when- ... (c) the votes cast in favour of the resolution, whether on a show of hands, or electronically or on a poll... are required to be not less than three times the number of the votes, if any, cast against the resolution by members so entitled and voting.[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: Defines the two main types of shareholder votes. An 'Ordinary Resolution' needs a simple majority (over 50% approval). A 'Special Resolution' needs a supermajority (at least 75% approval) to pass.[cite: 17]

title: Resolutions requiring special notice
text: Where, by any provision contained in this Act or in the articles of a company, special notice is required of any resolution, notice of the intention to move such resolution shall be given to the company by such number of members holding not less than one per cent. of total voting power or holding shares on which such aggregate sum not exceeding five lakh rupees, as may be prescribed, has been paid-up and the company shall give its members notice of the resolution in such manner as may be prescribed.[cite: 17]
plain_english_summary: Certain major actions (like firing an auditor or director) require 'Special Notice'. Shareholders holding at least 1% voting power or ₹5 Lakhs in shares must notify the company of their intent to move this resolution.[cite: 17]

title: Resolutions passed at adjourned meeting
text: Where a resolution is passed at an adjourned meeting of- (a) a company; or (b) the holders of any class of shares in a company; or (c) the Board of Directors of a company, the resolution shall, for all purposes, be treated as having been passed on the date on which it was in fact passed, and shall not be deemed to have been passed on any earlier date.[cite: 17]
plain_english_summary: If a meeting is delayed/adjourned to a later date, any decisions made at the delayed meeting are legally effective from that actual later date, not backdated to the original scheduled date.[cite: 17]

title: Resolutions and agreements to be filed
text: (1) A copy of every resolution or any agreement, in respect of matters specified in sub-section (3) together with the explanatory statement under section 102, if any, annexed to the notice calling the meeting in which the resolution is proposed, shall be filed with the Registrar within thirty days of the passing or making thereof in such manner and with such fees as may be prescribed...[cite: 17]

sub_structure.2: (2) If any company fails to file the resolution or the agreement under sub-section (1) before the expiry of the period specified therein, such company shall be liable to a penalty of ten thousand rupees and in case of continuing failure, with a further penalty of one hundred rupees for each day after the first during which such failure continues, subject to a maximum of two lakh rupees and every officer... shall be liable to a penalty of ten thousand rupees...[cite: 17]
sub_structure.3_a: (3) The provisions of this section shall apply to- (a) special resolutions;[cite: 17]
sub_structure.3_c: (c) any resolution of the Board of Directors of a company or agreement executed by a company, relating to the appointment, re-appointment or renewal of the appointment, or variation of the terms of appointment, of a managing director;[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: Whenever a startup passes a Special Resolution or signs major board agreements (like appointing a Managing Director), a copy must be filed with the ROC (via form MGT-14) within 30 days. Failing to do this results in a ₹10,000 fine plus daily penalties.[cite: 17]

title: Minutes of proceedings of general meeting, meeting of Board of Directors and other meeting and resolutions passed by postal ballot
text: (1) Every company shall cause minutes of the proceedings of every general meeting of any class of shareholders or creditors, and every resolution passed by postal ballot and every meeting of its Board of Directors or of every committee of the Board, to be prepared and signed in such manner as may be prescribed and kept within thirty days of the conclusion of every such meeting concerned, or passing of resolution by postal ballot in books kept for that purpose with their pages consecutively numbered.[cite: 17]

sub_structure.10: (10) Every company shall observe secretarial standards with respect to general and Board meetings specified by the Institute of Company Secretaries of India...[cite: 17]
sub_structure.11: (11) If any default is made in complying with the provisions of this section in respect of any meeting, the company shall be liable to a penalty of twenty-five thousand rupees and every officer of the company who is in default shall be liable to a penalty of five thousand rupees.[cite: 17]
sub_structure.12: (12) If a person is found guilty of tampering with the minutes of the proceedings of meeting, he shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years and with fine which shall not be less than twenty-five thousand rupees but which may extend to one lakh rupees.[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: Startups must create, sign, and safely store exact 'minutes' (written records) of every board and shareholder meeting within 30 days. Tampering with or altering these minutes is a severe crime punishable by up to 2 years in prison.[cite: 17]

title: Inspection of minute-books of general meeting
text: (1) The books containing the minutes of the proceedings of any general meeting of a company or of a resolution passed by postal ballot, shall- (a) be kept at the registered office of the company; and (b) be open, during business hours, to the inspection by any member without charge, subject to such reasonable restrictions as the company may, by its articles or in general meeting, impose, so, however, that not less than two hours in each business day are allowed for inspection.[cite: 17]

sub_structure.3: (3) If any inspection under sub-section (1) is refused, or if any copy required under sub-section (2) is not furnished within the time specified therein, the company shall be liable to a penalty of twenty-five thousand rupees and every officer of the company who is in default shall be liable to a penalty of five thousand rupees for each such refusal or default, as the case may be.[cite: 17]
sub_structure.4: (4) In the case of any such refusal or default, the Tribunal may... direct an immediate inspection of the minute-books or direct that the copy required shall forthwith be sent to the person requiring it.[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: Shareholders have a legal right to inspect the minute-books of general meetings for free at the company's registered office. If the startup refuses to let an investor see them, the company is slapped with a ₹25,000 penalty and the Tribunal can force them to hand over the copies.[cite: 17]

title: Maintenance and inspection of documents in electronic form
text: Without prejudice to any other provisions of this Act, any document, record, register, minutes, etc.,- (a) required to be kept by a company; or (b) allowed to be inspected or copies to be given to any person by a company under this Act, may be kept or inspected or copies given, as the case may be, in electronic form in such form and manner as may be prescribed.[cite: 17]
plain_english_summary: Startups are legally allowed to maintain their official records, minute books, and shareholder registers entirely in electronic/digital formats, rather than keeping physical paper binders.[cite: 17]

title: Report on annual general meeting
text: (1) Every listed public company shall prepare in the prescribed manner a report on each annual general meeting including the confirmation to the effect that the meeting was convened, held and conducted as per the provisions of this Act...[cite: 17]

sub_structure.2: (2) The company shall file with the Registrar a copy of the report referred to in sub-section (1) within thirty days of the conclusion of the annual general meeting...[cite: 17]
sub_structure.3: (3) If the company fails to file the report under sub-section (2) before the expiry of the period specified therein, such company shall be liable to a penalty of one lakh rupees and in case of continuing failure, with a further penalty of five hundred rupees for each day... and every officer of the company who is in default shall be liable to a penalty...[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: If a startup goes public, it must prepare a formal report confirming its AGM was conducted legally and file it with the ROC within 30 days. Late filing triggers an immediate ₹1 Lakh fine plus daily penalties.[cite: 17]

title: Applicability of this Chapter to One Person Company
text: (1) The provisions of section 98 and sections 100 to 111 (both inclusive) shall not apply to a One Person Company.[cite: 17]

sub_structure.3: (3) For the purposes of section 114, any business which is required to be transacted at an annual general meeting... it shall be sufficient if, in case of One Person Company, the resolution is communicated by the member to the company and entered in the minutes-book...[cite: 17]
sub_structure.4: (4) Notwithstanding anything in this Act, where there is only one director on the Board of Director of a One Person Company... it shall be sufficient if... the resolution by such director is entered in the minutes-book...[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: One Person Companies (OPCs) are exempt from the strict rules regarding holding general meetings, proxy voting, and calling EGMs. An OPC founder just needs to write their decisions in the minute-book and sign them to make them legally valid.[cite: 17]

title: Declaration of dividend
text: (1) No dividend shall be declared or paid by a company for any financial year except- (a) out of the profits of the company for that year arrived at after providing for depreciation... or out of the profits of the company for any previous financial year or years... or out of both:[cite: 17]

sub_structure.1_proviso_1: Provided that in computing profits any amount representing unrealised gains, notional gains or revaluation of assets... shall be excluded;[cite: 17]
sub_structure.3: (3) The Board of Directors of a company may declare interim dividend during any financial year... out of the surplus in the profit and loss account or out of profits of the financial year...[cite: 17]
sub_structure.4: (4) The amount of the dividend, including interim dividend, shall be deposited in a scheduled bank in a separate account within five days from the date of declaration of such dividend.[cite: 17]
sub_structure.6: (6) A company which fails to comply with the provisions of sections 73 and 74 shall not, so long as such failure continues, declare any dividend on its equity shares.[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: A startup can only pay dividends to its investors out of actual, realized profits (not 'paper' gains from revaluing assets) after accounting for depreciation. Once declared, the dividend money must be parked in a separate bank account within 5 days. Companies defaulting on public deposits cannot declare dividends.[cite: 17]

title: Unpaid Dividend Account
text: (1) Where a dividend has been declared by a company but has not been paid or claimed within thirty days from the date of the declaration... the company shall, within seven days from the date of expiry of the said period of thirty days, transfer the total amount of dividend which remains unpaid or unclaimed to a special account to be opened by the company in that behalf in any scheduled bank to be called the Unpaid Dividend Account.[cite: 17]

sub_structure.3: (3) If any default is made in transferring the total amount... to the Unpaid Dividend Account... it shall pay, from the date of such default, interest on so much of the amount as has not been transferred... at the rate of twelve per cent. per annum...[cite: 17]
sub_structure.5: (5) Any money transferred to the Unpaid Dividend Account of a company... which remains unpaid or unclaimed for a period of seven years... shall be transferred by the company along with interest accrued, if any, thereon to the Fund established under sub-section (1) of section 125...[cite: 17]
sub_structure.6: (6) All shares in respect of which dividend has not been paid or claimed for seven consecutive years or more shall be transferred by the company in the name of Investor Education and Protection Fund...[cite: 17]
sub_structure.7: (7) If a company fails to comply with any of the requirements of this section, such company shall be liable to a penalty of one lakh rupees and in case of continuing failure... subject to a maximum of ten lakh rupees...[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: If a shareholder doesn't claim their dividend within 30 days, the startup must move it to an 'Unpaid Dividend Account'. If the money remains unclaimed for 7 straight years, the company must surrender both the cash AND the underlying shares to a government fund (IEPF). Failing to follow these rules triggers hefty fines.[cite: 17]

title: Investor Education and Protection Fund
text: (1) The Central Government shall establish a Fund to be called the Investor Education and Protection Fund (herein referred to as the Fund).[cite: 17]

sub_structure.2_c: (2) There shall be credited to the Fund- ... (c) the amount in the Unpaid Dividend Account of companies transferred to the Fund under sub-section (5) of section 124;[cite: 17]
sub_structure.3_a: (3) The Fund shall be utilised for- (a) the refund in respect of unclaimed dividends, matured deposits, matured debentures, the application money due for refund and interest thereon;[cite: 17]
sub_structure.4: (4) Any person claiming to be entitled to the amount referred in sub-section (2) may apply to the authority constituted under sub-section (5) for the payment of the money claimed.[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: Creates the IEPF, a government fund that pools together unclaimed dividends, matured deposits, and abandoned shares from all companies. Investors who lost track of their assets can petition this authority to get their money or shares back.[cite: 17]

title: Right to dividend, rights shares and bonus shares to be held in abeyance pending registration of transfer of shares
text: Where any instrument of transfer of shares has been delivered to any company for registration and the transfer of such shares has not been registered by the company, it shall... (a) transfer the dividend in relation to such shares to the Unpaid Dividend Account... and (b) keep in abeyance in relation to such shares, any offer of rights shares... and any issue of fully paid-up bonus shares...[cite: 17]
plain_english_summary: If someone buys shares in a startup but the company hasn't officially updated its cap table yet, any dividends, bonus shares, or rights issues belonging to those shares must be frozen (held in abeyance) until the transfer is officially registered.[cite: 17]

title: Punishment for failure to distribute dividends
text: Where a dividend has been declared by a company but has not been paid or the warrant in respect thereof has not been posted within thirty days from the date of declaration to any shareholder... every director of the company shall, if he is knowingly a party to the default, be punishable with imprisonment which may extend to two years and with fine which shall not be less than one thousand rupees for every day... and the company shall be liable to pay simple interest at the rate of eighteen per cent. per annum...[cite: 17]

sub_structure.proviso: Provided that no offence under this section shall be deemed to have been committed: (a) where the dividend could not be paid by reason of the operation of any law; (b) where a shareholder has given directions to the company... and those directions cannot be complied with... (c) where there is a dispute regarding the right to receive the dividend;[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: Once a startup declares a dividend, it becomes a hard legal debt. Failing to pay it out within 30 days is a serious crime: directors face up to 2 years in prison and the company must pay a massive 18% penalty interest rate on the unpaid amount, unless there's an ongoing legal dispute over the shares.[cite: 17]

title: Books of account, etc., to be kept by company
text: (1) Every company shall prepare and keep at its registered office books of account and other relevant books and papers and financial statement for every financial year which give a true and fair view of the state of the affairs of the company... and such books shall be kept on accrual basis and according to the double entry system of accounting:[cite: 17]

sub_structure.1_proviso_2: Provided further that the company may keep such books of account or other relevant papers in electronic mode in such manner as may be prescribed.[cite: 17]
sub_structure.5: (5) The books of account of every company relating to a period of not less than eight financial years immediately preceding a financial year... shall be kept in good order:[cite: 17]
sub_structure.6: (6) If the managing director, the whole-time director in charge of finance, the Chief Financial Officer... contravenes such provisions... shall be punishable with fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees but which may extend to five lakh rupees.[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: Startups are legally required to maintain accurate, double-entry accounting records at their registered office (or digitally) and preserve these financial records for at least 8 years. If the CFO or directors fail to do this, they face personal fines up to ₹5 Lakhs.[cite: 17]

title: Financial statement
text: (1) The financial statements shall give a true and fair view of the state of affairs of the company or companies, comply with the accounting standards notified under section 133 and shall be in the form or forms as may be provided for different class or classes of companies in Schedule III:[cite: 17]

sub_structure.2: (2) At every annual general meeting of a company, the Board of Directors of the company shall lay before such meeting financial statements for the financial year.[cite: 17]
sub_structure.3: (3) Where a company has one or more subsidiaries or associate companies, it shall, in addition to financial statements provided under sub-section (2), prepare a consolidated financial statement of the company and of all the subsidiaries and associate companies...[cite: 17]
sub_structure.7: (7) If a company contravenes the provisions of this section, the managing director, the whole-time director in charge of finance, the Chief Financial Officer... shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year or with fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees but which may extend to five lakh rupees, or with both.[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: Startups must prepare annual financial statements (and consolidated statements if they have subsidiaries) that give a 'true and fair view' of the business and follow legal accounting standards. The Board must present these to shareholders at the AGM. Falsifying or failing to produce these records carries up to 1 year of prison time for the CFO/directors.[cite: 17]

title: Periodical financial results
text: The Central Government may, require such class or classes of unlisted companies, as may be prescribed,- (a) to prepare the financial results of the company on such periodical basis and in such form as may be prescribed; (b) to obtain approval of the Board of Directors and complete audit or limited review of such periodical financial results... and (c) file a copy with the Registrar within a period of thirty days of completion of the relevant period with such fees as may be prescribed.[cite: 17]
plain_english_summary: The government has the power to force specific types of large, unlisted private startups to prepare, audit, and file financial results more frequently than just once a year (e.g., quarterly or half-yearly).[cite: 17]

title: Re-opening of accounts on court's or Tribunal's orders
text: (1) A company shall not re-open its books of account and not recast its financial statements, unless an application in this regard is made by the Central Government, the Income-tax authorities, the Securities and Exchange Board... and an order is made by a court of competent jurisdiction or the Tribunal to the effect that- (i) the relevant earlier accounts were prepared in a fraudulent manner; or (ii) the affairs of the company were mismanaged during the relevant period, casting a doubt on the reliability of financial statements:[cite: 17]

sub_structure.3: (3) No order shall be made under sub-section (1) in respect of re-opening of books of account relating to a period earlier than eight financial years immediately preceding the current financial year:[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: A startup cannot secretly go back and rewrite its past financial statements. Past accounts can only be reopened and 'recast' if a court or Tribunal orders it, usually because tax authorities or SEBI suspect fraud or severe mismanagement. This look-back period is capped at 8 years.[cite: 17]

title: Voluntary revision of financial statements or Board's report
text: (1) If it appears to the directors of a company that- (a) the financial statement of the company; or (b) the report of the Board, do not comply with the provisions of section 129 or section 134 they may prepare revised financial statement or a revised report in respect of any of the three preceding financial years after obtaining approval of the Tribunal...[cite: 17]

sub_structure.1_proviso_2: Provided further that such revised financial statement or report shall not be prepared or filed more than once in a financial year:[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: If a startup's directors realize they made an honest mistake in their past financial statements or Board reports, they can voluntarily fix them. However, they can only revise the last 3 years, they must get the Tribunal's permission first, and they can only do this once per financial year.[cite: 17]

title: Constitution of National Financial Reporting Authority
text: (1) The Central Government may, by notification, constitute a National Financial Reporting Authority to provide for matters relating to accounting and auditing standards under this Act.[cite: 17]

sub_structure.2_a: (2) ...the National Financial Reporting Authority shall- (a) make recommendations to the Central Government on the formulation and laying down of accounting and auditing policies and standards for adoption by companies or class of companies or their auditors...[cite: 17]
sub_structure.4_a: (4) ...the National Financial Reporting Authority shall- (a) have the power to investigate, either suo motu or on a reference made to it by the Central Government... into the matters of professional or other misconduct committed by any member or firm of chartered accountants...[cite: 17]
sub_structure.4_c: (c) where professional or other misconduct is proved, have the power to make order for- (A) imposing penalty... (B) debarring the member or the firm from- I. being appointed as an auditor... for a minimum period of six months or such higher period not exceeding ten years...[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: Establishes the NFRA, an independent super-regulator for auditors. The NFRA sets the accounting rules startups must follow and has sweeping powers to investigate, fine, and ban auditing firms (Chartered Accountants) that commit misconduct or help companies hide financial fraud.[cite: 17]

title: Central Government to prescribe accounting standards
text: The Central Government may prescribe the standards of accounting or any addendum thereto, as recommended by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, constituted under section 3 of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 (38 of 1949), in consultation with and after examination of the recommendations made by the National Financial Reporting Authority:[cite: 17]
plain_english_summary: The Central Government is legally responsible for dictating the specific accounting standards (like Ind AS) that startups and companies must use, based on recommendations from the ICAI and NFRA.[cite: 17]

title: Financial statement, Board's report, etc.
text: (1) The financial statement, including consolidated financial statement, if any, shall be approved by the Board of Directors before they are signed on behalf of the Board by the chairperson of the company... and the Chief Executive Officer, the Chief Financial Officer and the company secretary...[cite: 17]

sub_structure.3: (3) There shall be attached to statements laid before a company in general meeting, a report by its Board of Directors, which shall include- ... (c) Directors' Responsibility Statement; (ca) details in respect of frauds reported by auditors... (g) particulars of loans, guarantees or investments... (h) particulars of contracts or arrangements with related parties...[cite: 17]
sub_structure.5: (5) The Directors' Responsibility Statement referred to in clause (c) of sub-section (3) shall state that- (a) in the preparation of the annual accounts, the applicable accounting standards had been followed... (c) the directors had taken proper and sufficient care for the maintenance of adequate accounting records... for preventing and detecting fraud...[cite: 17]
sub_structure.8: (8) If a company is in default in complying with the provisions of this section, the company shall be liable to a penalty of three lakh rupees and every officer of the company who is in default shall be liable to a penalty of fifty thousand rupees.[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: The startup's Board must formally approve and attach a detailed 'Board's Report' to the annual financials. This report forces directors to publicly declare they took steps to prevent fraud, followed accounting rules, and disclosed all related-party transactions (like contracts with the founders' family members). Failing to do so carries strict fines.[cite: 17]

title: Corporate Social Responsibility
text: (1) Every company having net worth of rupees five hundred crore or more, or turnover of rupees one thousand crore or more or a net profit of rupees five crore or more during the immediately preceding financial year shall constitute a Corporate Social Responsibility Committee of the Board...[cite: 17]

sub_structure.5: (5) The Board of every company referred to in sub-section (1), shall ensure that the company spends, in every financial year, at least two per cent. of the average net profits of the company made during the three immediately preceding financial years... in pursuance of its Corporate Social Responsibility Policy:[cite: 17]
sub_structure.6: (6) Any amount remaining unspent under sub-section (5), pursuant to any ongoing project... shall be transferred by the company within a period of thirty days from the end of the financial year to a special account... failing which, the company shall transfer the same to a Fund specified in Schedule VII...[cite: 17]
sub_structure.7: (7) If a company is in default in complying with the provisions of sub-section (5) or sub-section (6), the company shall be liable to a penalty of twice the amount required to be transferred by the company to the Fund... or one crore rupees, whichever is less, and every officer... shall be liable to a penalty...[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: Highly profitable startups (e.g., net profit > ₹5 Crore) are legally mandated to spend 2% of their average net profits on Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) activities. Unspent money must be transferred to government-approved funds. Falsifying or ignoring CSR mandates carries massive financial penalties.[cite: 17]

title: Right of member to copies of audited financial statement
text: (1) ...a copy of the financial statements, including consolidated financial statements, if any, auditor's report and every other document required by law to be annexed or attached to the financial statements, which are to be laid before a company in its general meeting, shall be sent to every member of the company, to every trustee for the debenture-holder... not less than twenty-one days before the date of the meeting:[cite: 17]

sub_structure.3: (3) If any default is made in complying with the provisions of this section, the company shall be liable to a penalty of twenty-five thousand rupees and every officer of the company who is in default shall be liable to a penalty of five thousand rupees.[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: A startup must send its audited financials and board reports to all shareholders and investors at least 21 days before the Annual General Meeting so they have time to review the numbers. Failing to distribute these carries a penalty.[cite: 17]

title: Copy of financial statement to be filed with Registrar
text: (1) A copy of the financial statements, including consolidated financial statement, if any, along with all the documents which are required to be or attached to such financial statements under this Act, duly adopted at the annual general meeting of the company, shall be filed with the Registrar within thirty days of the date of annual general meeting...[cite: 17]

sub_structure.3: (3) If a company fails to file the copy of the financial statements... before the expiry of the period specified therein the company shall be liable to a penalty of ten thousand rupees and in case of continuing failure, with a further penalty of one hundred rupees for each day... subject to a maximum of two lakh rupees, and the managing director and the Chief Financial Officer... shall be liable to a penalty of ten thousand rupees...[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: After the shareholders approve the financials at the AGM, the startup has 30 days to officially file them with the government (ROC) via form AOC-4. Late filing triggers immediate and accumulating daily penalties for both the company and the founders/CFO.[cite: 17]

title: Internal Audit
text: (1) Such class or classes of companies as may be prescribed shall be required to appoint an internal auditor, who shall either be a chartered accountant or a cost accountant, or such other professional as may be decided by the Board to conduct internal audit of the functions and activities of the company.[cite: 17]

sub_structure.2: (2) The Central Government may, by rules, prescribe the manner and the intervals in which the internal audit shall be conducted and reported to the Board.[cite: 17]

plain_english_summary: Larger startups (based on revenue or debt thresholds set by the government) must appoint a dedicated Internal Auditor (usually a CA) whose sole job is to constantly check the company's internal controls and report findings directly to the Board.[cite: 17]

title: Appointment of auditors
text: (1) Subject to the provisions of this Chapter, every company shall, at the first annual general meeting, appoint an individual or a firm as an auditor who shall hold office from the conclusion of that meeting till the conclusion of its sixth annual general meeting...[cite: 12]

sub_structure.2: (2) No listed company or a company belonging to such class or classes of companies as may be prescribed, shall appoint or re-appoint- (a) an individual as auditor for more than one term of five consecutive years; and (b) an audit firm as auditor for more than two terms of five consecutive years...[cite: 12]
sub_structure.6: (6) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), the first auditor of a company, other than a Government company, shall be appointed by the Board of Directors within thirty days from the date of registration of the company...[cite: 12]
sub_structure.8_i: (8) Any casual vacancy in the office of an auditor shall- (i) in the case of a company other than a company whose accounts are subject to audit by an auditor appointed by the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India, be filled by the Board of Directors within thirty days...[cite: 12]

plain_english_summary: Startups must appoint their first auditor within 30 days of incorporation. At the first AGM, an auditor is appointed for a 5-year term. For larger/listed companies, auditors must be mandatorily rotated out after their term limits to ensure independent financial oversight.[cite: 12]

title: Removal, resignation of auditor and giving of special notice
text: (1) The auditor appointed under section 139 may be removed from his office before the expiry of his term only by a special resolution of the company, after obtaining the previous approval of the Central Government in that behalf in the prescribed manner:[cite: 12]

sub_structure.2: (2) The auditor who has resigned from the company shall file within a period of thirty days from the date of resignation, a statement in the prescribed form with the company and the Registrar...[cite: 12]
sub_structure.3: (3) If the auditor does not comply with the provisions of sub-section (2), he or it shall be liable to a penalty of fifty thousand rupees or an amount equal to the remuneration of the auditor, whichever is less, and in case of continuing failure, with a further penalty... subject to a maximum of two lakh rupees.[cite: 12]
sub_structure.5: (5) Without prejudice to any action under the provisions of this Act... the Tribunal either suo motu or on an application... if it is satisfied that the auditor of a company has, whether directly or in directly, acted in a fraudulent manner or abetted or colluded in any fraud... it may, by order, direct the company to change its auditors:[cite: 12]

plain_english_summary: Removing an auditor before their term expires is deliberately difficult and requires both 75% shareholder approval and Central Government permission. If an auditor resigns, they must officially notify the ROC within 30 days, or face heavy fines. The Tribunal can forcefully ban fraudulent auditors for 5 years.[cite: 12]

title: Eligibility, qualifications and disqualifications of auditors
text: (1) A person shall be eligible for appointment as an auditor of a company only if he is a chartered accountant:[cite: 12]

sub_structure.3_b: (b) an officer or employee of the company;[cite: 12]
sub_structure.3_d_i: (d) a person who, or his relative or partner- (i) is holding any security of or interest in the company or its subsidiary... Provided that the relative may hold security or interest in the company of face value not exceeding one thousand rupees or such sum as may be prescribed;[cite: 12]
sub_structure.3_g: (g) a person who is in full time employment elsewhere or a person or a partner of a firm holding appointment as its auditor, if such persons or partner is at the date of such appointment or reappointment holding appointment as auditor of more than twenty companies;[cite: 12]
sub_structure.4: (4) Where a person appointed as an auditor of a company incurs any of the disqualifications mentioned in sub-section (3) after his appointment, he shall vacate his office as such auditor...[cite: 12]
